title: World War II: The War That Changed the World

lines.text: In the summer of nineteen thirty nine, Europe stood on the edge of another catastrophe, only twenty years after the First World War.
The peace settlement had left anger, economic hardship, and political instability across several countries, while dictators promised national revival.
In Germany, Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party had dismantled democracy, persecuted minorities, and rebuilt the armed forces in defiance of treaties.
Across Europe, governments watched Germany expand its territory, first through pressure and annexation, then through increasingly dangerous threats.
Britain and France hoped diplomacy could prevent another war, but concessions did not satisfy Hitler's ambitions or protect Europe's smaller states.
To understand the conflict, we must follow the choices, invasions, alliances, and turning points that transformed a regional crisis into a world war.
Many people remembered the First World War as a warning, but economic collapse and political extremism made compromise harder and made democratic institutions more fragile.
On the first of September nineteen thirty nine, German forces invaded Poland from the west, using aircraft, tanks, and fast moving ground units.
Two days later, Britain and France declared war on Germany, turning the attack into a European war that would soon spread much farther.
German forces used coordinated tactics often called Blitzkrieg, combining air power, armour, and infantry to disrupt communication and overwhelm defences.
On the seventeenth of September, the Soviet Union invaded eastern Poland under the terms of a secret agreement with Nazi Germany.
Poland was divided between two occupying powers, and its people faced repression, deportation, forced labour, and the destruction of political independence.
Although the campaign ended quickly, Polish soldiers continued fighting abroad, while the government in exile helped the Allies throughout the war.
The invasion relied on speed and surprise, but it also exposed civilians to bombing, displacement, and the collapse of ordinary life in towns and villages.
In nineteen forty, Germany attacked Denmark and Norway, then launched a major offensive through the Low Countries and into France.
German armoured units crossed the Ardennes, bypassing strong French defences and pushing Allied forces toward the English Channel.
Hundreds of thousands of British and French troops were evacuated from Dunkirk, a remarkable rescue that preserved much of Britain's army.
France signed an armistice in June nineteen forty, and German occupation reshaped daily life across much of western Europe.
Britain remained outside German control, protected by the English Channel and determined to continue the fight despite severe military danger.
Across occupied countries, resistance networks gathered intelligence, sheltered fugitives, published underground newspapers, and supported Allied operations.
Occupation was not identical everywhere, yet censorship, forced labour, food shortages, imprisonment, and fear became familiar realities for millions of people.
During the summer and autumn of nineteen forty, Germany tried to gain control of the skies before attempting an invasion of Britain.
The Royal Air Force defended the country against waves of German aircraft, while radar stations helped detect incoming raids.
Airfields, factories, ports, and cities became targets, and civilians endured air raids during the period known as the Blitz.
British pilots were outnumbered at times, but effective warning systems, repairs, aircraft production, and determined crews helped sustain the defence.
Germany failed to destroy the RAF or secure the air superiority needed for an invasion across the Channel.
The planned invasion was postponed, and Britain remained a base from which the Allies would later return to western Europe.
The battle also showed how technology, intelligence, training, logistics, and the work of ground crews could matter as much as individual courage in the air.
In June nineteen forty one, Hitler launched Operation Barbarossa, a massive invasion of the Soviet Union that opened the largest land front in history.
German armies advanced rapidly, capturing territory and millions of Soviet prisoners, while Soviet forces retreated and destroyed supplies behind them.
The invasion was shaped by ideology as well as military strategy, and Nazi occupation brought mass murder, starvation, and brutal racial persecution.
Despite enormous losses, the Soviet Union moved factories east, mobilised reserves, and continued producing tanks, aircraft, weapons, and ammunition.
The German advance stalled before Moscow, while winter, stretched supply lines, Soviet resistance, and strategic mistakes weakened the invaders.
At Leningrad, civilians endured a devastating siege, while the Eastern Front became a struggle of immense human cost and industrial endurance.
Millions of Soviet civilians and soldiers suffered, and the German campaign included deliberate starvation policies and mass shootings carried out by mobile killing units.
On the seventh of December nineteen forty one, Japanese aircraft attacked the American naval base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii.
The attack damaged battleships and aircraft, killed more than two thousand Americans, and shocked the United States into entering the war.
Japan soon expanded across Southeast Asia and the Pacific, attacking territories held by Britain, the Netherlands, and the United States.
Germany and Italy declared war on the United States, linking the European and Pacific conflicts even more closely.
American factories shifted toward enormous wartime production, supplying ships, aircraft, vehicles, food, and equipment to Allied forces around the world.
The conflict was now truly global, fought across oceans, deserts, jungles, cities, and vast stretches of the European and Asian continents.
Across the Pacific, the distances were immense, and control of airfields, ports, shipping routes, and islands shaped the strategy of both sides.
In June nineteen forty two, the Battle of Midway became a major turning point in the Pacific, as American forces sank four Japanese aircraft carriers.
On the Eastern Front, the Battle of Stalingrad ended with the surrender of a major German army in February nineteen forty three.
The Allied victory in North Africa helped open the way for the invasion of Sicily and then mainland Italy.
At sea, convoys and escort groups fought to keep vital supplies moving across the Atlantic against German submarines.
Codebreakers, radar operators, engineers, nurses, factory workers, and resistance groups all contributed to the Allied war effort.
These victories did not end the war, but they shifted momentum and made the defeat of the Axis powers increasingly possible.
Allied leaders also had to coordinate different armies, economies, and political goals, while planning how to supply forces far from their home countries.
On the sixth of June nineteen forty four, Allied forces landed on the beaches of Normandy in northern France during Operation Overlord.
Thousands of ships and aircraft supported the invasion, while soldiers from several Allied nations fought to establish a foothold in Europe.
The Normandy campaign was difficult and costly, but the Allies broke out of the beachhead and liberated Paris in August.
From the east, Soviet armies pushed German forces back through occupied territory, while Allied troops advanced from the west.
Germany faced shortages, bombing, damaged transport networks, and pressure on multiple fronts, yet fighting continued with terrible consequences.
In April nineteen forty five, Soviet forces entered Berlin, and Hitler died as the Nazi regime collapsed around him.
The landings depended on careful deception, weather forecasts, naval gunfire, airborne troops, engineers, medics, and the difficult work of moving supplies ashore.
Even after Germany surrendered in May nineteen forty five, the war continued across the Pacific, where Japanese forces resisted Allied advances.
Battles at Iwo Jima and Okinawa showed how costly an invasion of the Japanese home islands might become.
The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on the sixth of August and Nagasaki on the ninth of August nineteen forty five.
The Soviet Union also entered the war against Japan, attacking Japanese forces in Manchuria in August.
Japan announced its surrender on the fifteenth of August, and the formal surrender was signed on the second of September.
The Second World War had ended, but millions of families were grieving, cities lay damaged, and survivors faced the long work of rebuilding.
The decision to use atomic weapons remains deeply debated, and historians continue to examine its military, political, and human consequences.
World War Two killed tens of millions of people, including soldiers and civilians, and the Holocaust murdered six million Jewish people.
Nazi Germany also persecuted and murdered Roma people, disabled people, Polish civilians, Soviet prisoners of war, and many other groups.
The United Nations was founded in nineteen forty five in an effort to support international cooperation and prevent another global conflict.
Europe's old empires weakened, the United States and Soviet Union emerged as rival superpowers, and the Cold War soon began.
War crimes trials confronted some of the leaders responsible, while refugees, displaced families, and survivors searched for homes and justice.
World War Two was not simply a sequence of battles; it was a warning about dictatorship, aggressive nationalism, racism, and the cost of unchecked power.
After the fighting, international agreements and institutions could not erase the damage, but they reflected a determination to build a more stable future.
